script.opening: (Calm, controlled, firm; has printed pages from the app beside him.) "I've been looking at my records online and I want some things taken out. There's an old note about 'alcohol dependence' — that was years ago, I've sorted myself out, and frankly it's nobody's business and it's stigmatising me. And there's an allergy listed that I haven't even got. Just delete them both, please. They're wrong and they're causing me problems."

facts.text: Record says "penicillin allergy — rash" from about 10 years ago. "I've never reacted to anything. I don't know where it came from." If asked: had amoxicillin from a dentist two years ago with no problem. Never had a rash, swelling or breathing problem with any medicine.

Entry from 7 years ago: "alcohol dependence". If asked what happened then: drinking heavily after a divorce, saw a GP, went to the local alcohol service, had a supported detox at home. Has drunk only occasionally since — "a pint at a wedding". If asked: "I'm fine. Well for years. That's the point." Liver tests normal last year.

"It follows me around. Work, insurance, medicals. People see a label and judge me, and I'm not that person any more." Applying for a promotion that needs an occupational health report, and for life insurance. A nurse at a recent hospital appointment mentioned "your alcohol history" in front of his new partner.
"That someone reads it and decides who I am. I want a clean slate." Doesn't know who can see his record or that he can see reports before they are sent.
Well, no regular medicines. Works as a logistics team leader. Lives with partner, Jo. Non-smoker. Runs three times a week.

Calm but determined; not aggressive. "It's my information." If told flatly no, become frustrated: "So you won't do it." Listens if the doctor explains why with respect. Pleased the allergy will be checked: "Good. That's one." Asks: "And if I'm still not happy?" Brightens on hearing about seeing reports first: "I didn't know I could see it first. That helps." Accepts adding his own statement.

ice.ideas: "Both entries are wrong and should just be deleted — it's my record."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — shame about the past and fear that the label will cost him the promotion and insurance and change how his new partner and others see him; he is proud of his recovery and feels it isn't reflected.

cues: "It's causing me problems." — invites asking what problems.
"I'm not that person any more." — pride in recovery to acknowledge.
"Who can actually see this?" — worry about confidentiality, if explored.

checkpoints.text: SEPARATES the two requests — treating the disputed ALLERGY as a potential factual inaccuracy to verify and correct (also a safety issue), and the historical alcohol-dependence diagnosis as an accurately-recorded professional opinion that is generally annotated rather than erased

Applies the DATA-PROTECTION framework correctly: UK GDPR Article 16 right to rectification of INACCURATE data (response within one month); disputed OPINION is annotated with the patient’s comment rather than deleted; NO absolute right to erasure of accurate records needed for care/medico-legal reasons

Upholds RECORD INTEGRITY — no falsification, deletion-to-rewrite-history or back-dating; any change made transparently with an audit trail — and recognises that removing accurate information to mislead third parties would be a probity breach

VERIFIES the disputed allergy against the source (original entry, letters, prescribing history) and then CORRECTS it with a note and audit trail rather than deleting it (NHS England guidance), recognising the clinical safety implication of an inaccurate allergy record

Offers the legitimate OPTIONS: add the patient’s statement/disagreement and note his recovery so the record reflects the current picture; explain formal rectification request, complaints process and the ICO route; and reassure accurately about confidentiality/third-party access (consent for employer/insurer reports, with narrow legal exceptions; Access to Medical Reports Act 1988 right to see a report before it is sent) — documenting the discussion

Explores empathically the REASON behind the request (stigma, specific harm, shame, privacy), validates his recovery and the harm of stigma, and maintains the therapeutic relationship despite not simply complying
Explains transparently and respectfully what can and cannot be done and WHY — avoiding both blunt refusal and improper agreement to delete — and checks his understanding

Safety-nets and follows up: corrects the allergy and flags it, sets out the next steps/options and timeframe for the disputed entry, documents the conversation, signposts formal routes, and offers review — lawful, transparent handling that preserves integrity and the relationship

worked.txt: "Thank you for raising this directly — your record matters and you have every right to question it. Let me take the two things separately, because they’re actually quite different, and I want to be straight with you about each."

"The allergy first: if that’s listed in error, that’s not only unfair, it’s a safety risk — so let’s check it properly — I’ll look back at where it came from, the hospital letters and your prescriptions — and if it turns out it was recorded in error, I’ll correct it, with a note explaining how we checked, so the record shows the change rather than it just vanishing. That one I can put right."

"The alcohol entry is different. It was a genuine record of what was happening and the care given at the time — so I can’t simply erase it, because the notes have to stay a truthful account, and I’m not allowed to delete accurate clinical history. I know that’s not what you hoped to hear, and I want to explain what I CAN do."

"Can I ask what’s behind this — is it the stigma, or is it causing a specific problem, like with work or insurance? … That makes complete sense, and your recovery is genuinely something to be proud of. The label shouldn’t define you."

"Here’s what we can do: I can add a clear note — in your words if you like — saying you dispute it and that you’ve been well and abstinent for years, so anyone reading sees the up-to-date picture. You can also make a formal correction request, and if you’re unhappy with the outcome there’s a complaints route and an external regulator. And importantly — an employer or insurer can’t get a report from us without your consent, apart from rare legal situations like a court order, and by law you can ask to see any report about you before it’s sent, ask for corrections, or add your own statement."

"I’ll check the allergy against the old records and correct it with a note once it’s verified, add whatever statement you’d like about the alcohol entry, and write up our conversation. Have a think about the formal request — take the information away — and come back if you want help with it. Does that feel like a fair way forward?"

f.learning: A request to amend the medical record is a professional/data-protection dilemma that turns on separating CORRECTION OF FACT from ERASURE OF ACCURATE RECORD. Here there are two requests: a disputed ALLERGY entry, which is a potential FACTUAL INACCURACY that should be verified first and then corrected with an audit trail (NHS England guidance on amending records) (an inaccurate allergy is also a clinical SAFETY issue); and a historical "alcohol dependence" diagnosis, which is an accurately-recorded professional OPINION/record of care that is generally NOT simply deleted even though the patient has recovered and finds it stigmatising. Under UK GDPR (Article 16)/Data Protection Act 2018, patients have a right to RECTIFICATION of inaccurate personal data (response within one month, Article 12), but a disputed professional OPINION is typically ANNOTATED with the patient’s comment rather than erased (an opinion accurately recorded as having been held is not "inaccurate"), and there is NO absolute right to erasure of health records needed for ongoing care or medico-legal/public-interest reasons. The record must remain a truthful, contemporaneous account: entries are not deleted to rewrite history, any agreed change is made transparently with an audit trail, and removing accurate information to mislead third parties (insurers/employers) would be a serious probity breach. Explore empathically WHY the patient wants the change — stigma, a concrete harm, shame, privacy — validate his recovery and the harm of stigma, and offer the legitimate options: correct the factual error, add the patient’s own statement and note his recovery so the record reflects the current picture, explain formal rectification/complaints/ICO routes, and reassure accurately that reports for employers or insurers need his consent (with narrow legal exceptions such as a court order) and that the Access to Medical Reports Act 1988 lets him see a report before it is sent, request corrections or attach a statement — all documented. The aim is lawful, transparent handling that preserves both record integrity and the therapeutic relationship, avoiding blunt refusal and improper deletion alike.

knowledge.guideline: UK GDPR Articles 16 and 17 · ICO guidance on the accuracy principle · NHS England: Amending patient and service user records · GMC Good medical practice (2024) · GMC Confidentiality (2017) · Access to Medical Reports Act 1988
knowledge.summary: Separate a possible factual error from a disputed but accurate clinical entry. Verify and correct the allergy with an audit trail; annotate, rather than erase, the historical diagnosis; explain his rights and routes openly.

points.t: UK GDPR Article 16 gives a right to have inaccurate personal data corrected. The ICO’s accuracy guidance: a record of an opinion is not inaccurate if it correctly records the opinion held at the time; where the patient disagrees, record his view alongside it.
UK GDPR Article 17 allows erasure in some circumstances, but it does not apply where processing is needed for health care or for public-health reasons. Accurate clinical history is kept.

NHS England guidance: even inaccurate information is not simply deleted; it is corrected or marked, with the reason and an audit trail, because others may have relied on it. Seek information-governance advice if deletion is ever considered.

Check the source before changing it: the original entry, hospital letters and prescribing history. If it was recorded in error, correct it with a note of how this was verified. Removing a true allergy on request is a safety risk.
Respond to a rectification request within one month (UK GDPR Article 12). If he is unhappy, he can use the practice complaints procedure and then complain to the ICO.

A GP report for an employer or insurer needs his consent. Under the Access to Medical Reports Act 1988 he can ask to see it before it is sent, ask for corrections, or attach a statement. Records must be honest and not misleading (GMC Good medical practice, 2024).

model.text: Hello Mr Salter, I’m Dr Lee. I understand you’ve been looking at your records. Tell me what you found.

There’s an old note about alcohol dependence. That was years ago, I’ve sorted myself out, and it’s nobody’s business. And there’s an allergy I haven’t got. Just delete them both, please. They’re causing me problems.

Thank you for raising it directly — you have every right to question what’s in your record. You’ve mentioned two things, and they’re quite different, so I’d like to take them one at a time and be straight with you about each. Is that okay?
model.why: Validates and separates the two requests

model.text: Fine. As long as they get sorted.
Let’s start with the allergy. Can you tell me what’s listed and whether you’ve ever taken that medicine?
model.why: Gathers facts to verify the allergy

model.text: I’ve never reacted to anything. I don’t know where it came from.

I’ll look at when it was added and whether there’s a hospital letter or prescription behind it. If it was put on in error, I’ll correct it. It matters for your safety both ways — a wrong allergy can stop you getting the right treatment.
model.why: Verifies before correcting; frames as safety

model.text: Good. That’s one.
Now the alcohol entry. You said it’s causing problems. Can you tell me what’s happened?
model.why: Explores the reason behind the request

model.text: It follows me around. Work, insurance, medicals. People see a label and judge me, and I’m not that person any more.
That sounds really frustrating, especially when you’ve worked hard to get well. How are things with alcohol now?
I’m fine. Well for years. That’s the point.
What worries you most about the entry staying there?
That someone reads it and decides who I am. I want a clean slate.
And you were hoping I could delete both today?
Yes. It’s my information.

It is your information, and you have rights over it. If something is wrong, like the allergy may be, you have a right to have it corrected. The alcohol entry is different: it was a record of what was happening and the care you had at the time. I can’t erase an accurate part of your medical history, because the record has to stay a true account.
So you won’t do it.
I can’t delete it, and I know that’s not what you wanted to hear. But I don’t want to leave it there. The record should also show where you are now. That part I can change.
model.why: Acknowledges disappointment and moves to options

model.text: Go on.

First, I can add a clear entry today recording that you dispute the old entry and that you’ve been well for years — in your own words if you like — so anyone reading sees the current picture. Second, you can make a formal written request, which the practice must answer within a month.
model.why: Offers annotation and the formal route

model.text: And if I’m still not happy?
Then there’s the practice complaints process, and after that the Information Commissioner’s Office, which regulates this. I’ll give you the details.

About work and insurance: employers and insurers can’t get a report from us without your consent. If one asks, you have the right to see the report before it’s sent, ask for corrections, and attach your own statement. I would have to be honest in any report, but I can make sure it reflects your recovery.
model.why: Accurate confidentiality and Access to Medical Reports Act advice

model.text: I didn’t know I could see it first. That helps.
Which would you like to start with — adding your statement now, or thinking about the formal request?
Add the statement now. I’ll think about the rest.

Then here’s the plan: I’ll check the allergy entry today and let you know by the end of the week what I found and what I’ve changed. I’ll add your statement, and I’ll document our conversation. If you want help with a formal request, come back to me.
Just so I’m sure I’ve explained it clearly — what’s your understanding of what we can and can’t do?
The allergy gets fixed if it’s wrong. The old note stays, but my side goes on too, and I can see any report before it goes. It’s not what I wanted, but it’s fair.

social.t: Labels about alcohol can follow people long after recovery. Acknowledge this and make sure the record shows his current status.

legal.t: Right to rectification (Article 16); right to erasure is limited where data are needed for health care (Article 17); respond within one month (Article 12). Complaints can go to the ICO.
For reports his own doctor writes for an employer or insurer: consent is needed, and he may see the report before it is sent, ask for corrections, or attach a statement.
Alcohol dependence is covered by DVLA Assessing fitness to drive. Changing the record does not change what a driver must declare; answer honestly if he asks.

professional.t: Records must be accurate and not altered to mislead (GMC Good medical practice, 2024). Corrections are made openly with an audit trail (NHS England: Amending patient and service user records).
Disclosure to employers or insurers needs consent; exceptions exist, such as a court order (GMC Confidentiality, 2017). Don’t promise that nobody will ever see his record.

community.t: ICO website for his data-protection rights; the practice privacy notice and complaints procedure.

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you know the difference between correcting and erasing, and whether you can say no to part of a request and keep the relationship.

items.fail: Treating both requests as the same and deleting or refusing both.
items.why: A factual error has a right to rectification; an accurate opinion does not have a right to erasure. Merging them is a knowledge failure.
items.fix: Say out loud that these are two different requests, and deal with each.

items.fail: Removing the allergy because he says he doesn’t have it.
items.why: A true allergy removed is a safety risk. Verification comes first.
items.fix: Check the original entry, letters and prescribing; correct with a note of how it was verified.

items.fail: Promising that nobody outside the practice will ever see his record.
items.why: There are exceptions, and reports he consents to must be honest.
items.fix: Explain consent, his right to see reports first, and that a report can reflect his recovery.

items.fail: Launching into data-protection law before asking why he wants the change.
items.why: The driver is stigma. Without exploring it, the explanation sounds like a brush-off.
items.fix: Ask what problems the entry has caused, and acknowledge his recovery.

items.why: Examiners mark down refusals without reasons or alternatives.
items.fix: Explain why, then offer what you can do: his statement, formal routes, and report rights.

items.fail: Ending without a timescale or documentation.
items.why: He leaves unsure what will happen.
items.fix: Give a date for the allergy outcome, document the discussion, and check understanding.

wordPics.pass: Separates the two requests; verifies and corrects the allergy; explains why the historical entry stays; offers to add his statement; documents.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus: explores the stigma and validates his recovery; explains rectification, complaints and ICO routes and the one-month response; explains consent and the Access to Medical Reports Act; keeps the relationship intact and checks understanding.

avoid.why: A blanket refusal is inaccurate and ends the conversation.

avoid.instead: “Let me check where the allergy came from first, and explain why the older entry has to stay.”

social.t: Labels about alcohol can follow people long after recovery. Acknowledge this and make sure the record shows his current status.

legal.t: Right to rectification (Article 16); right to erasure is limited where data are needed for health care (Article 17); respond within one month (Article 12). Complaints can go to the ICO.
For reports his own doctor writes for an employer or insurer: consent is needed, and he may see the report before it is sent, ask for corrections, or attach a statement.
Alcohol dependence is covered by DVLA Assessing fitness to drive. Changing the record does not change what a driver must declare; answer honestly if he asks.

professional.t: Records must be accurate and not altered to mislead (GMC Good medical practice, 2024). Corrections are made openly with an audit trail (NHS England: Amending patient and service user records).
Disclosure to employers or insurers needs consent; exceptions exist, such as a court order (GMC Confidentiality, 2017). Don’t promise that nobody will ever see his record.

community.t: ICO website for his data-protection rights; the practice privacy notice and complaints procedure.

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Two different requests: a possible factual error (allergy) to verify and rectify, and an accurate historical clinical entry (alcohol dependence) that is annotated with his view and recovery rather than erased.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of your record as a diary written at the time. If a date or fact is wrong, we fix it and note the fix. We can’t tear out a page that was true then — but we can add today’s page showing where you are now.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve worked hard to get well, and it feels unfair that an old label follows you. Let’s make sure the record shows who you are now.”
management.psychosocial: Validate his recovery; explain his rights over third-party reports; keep the door open for a formal request.

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you know the difference between correcting and erasing, and whether you can say no to part of a request and keep the relationship.

items.fail: Treating both requests as the same and deleting or refusing both.
items.why: A factual error has a right to rectification; an accurate opinion does not have a right to erasure. Merging them is a knowledge failure.
items.fix: Say out loud that these are two different requests, and deal with each.

items.fail: Removing the allergy because he says he doesn’t have it.
items.why: A true allergy removed is a safety risk. Verification comes first.
items.fix: Check the original entry, letters and prescribing; correct with a note of how it was verified.

items.fail: Promising that nobody outside the practice will ever see his record.
items.why: There are exceptions, and reports he consents to must be honest.
items.fix: Explain consent, his right to see reports first, and that a report can reflect his recovery.

items.fail: Launching into data-protection law before asking why he wants the change.
items.why: The driver is stigma. Without exploring it, the explanation sounds like a brush-off.
items.fix: Ask what problems the entry has caused, and acknowledge his recovery.

items.why: Examiners mark down refusals without reasons or alternatives.
items.fix: Explain why, then offer what you can do: his statement, formal routes, and report rights.

items.fail: Ending without a timescale or documentation.
items.why: He leaves unsure what will happen.
items.fix: Give a date for the allergy outcome, document the discussion, and check understanding.
